rubric.how: Name one use, such as making light alloys used in aircraft or flares and fireworks.

rubric.why: Awards the second mark for another valid use.
rubric.how: Name another use of magnesium.

modelAnswer: Magnesium is used to make light alloys for aircraft and other lightweight structures.

items.followUp: Compare Rutherford’s atomic model with Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Both models contain a central, positively charged nucleus; this is a key feature of the comparison.
rubric.how: State that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

rubric.why: Identifies the electron motion in the models.
rubric.how: State that electrons revolve around the nucleus.

rubric.why: The fixed energy levels are the distinctive addition made by Bohr.
rubric.how: Explain that Bohr placed electrons in fixed orbits or shells with definite energies, unlike Rutherford’s model.

rubric.why: Shows the instability problem in Rutherford’s model and how Bohr addressed it.
rubric.how: State that Rutherford’s orbiting electrons would radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, whereas Bohr’s electrons do not radiate energy in fixed orbits.

rubric.why: Recognises Bohr’s explanation of the line spectrum through changes between energy levels.
rubric.how: State that electrons absorb or emit definite amounts of energy when they jump between Bohr’s energy levels, explaining line spectra.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus, with electrons revolving around it.
In Rutherford’s model, electrons could revolve at any distance; he did not propose fixed energy levels.
According to Rutherford’s model, revolving electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so it could not explain atomic stability.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus only in fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
Electrons in these stationary orbits do not radiate energy; they absorb or emit definite energy when they move between orbits, explaining line spectra.

items.followUp: Define physical chemistry and biochemistry, and state one use of each.

rubric.why: Defines industrial chemistry by its focus on chemical manufacture and processes on an industrial scale.
rubric.how: Define it as the branch dealing with the manufacture of chemicals and chemical products on a large scale.

rubric.why: Gives a relevant application of industrial chemistry.
rubric.how: State that it is used to manufacture useful products such as fertilizers, medicines or cement.

rubric.why: Defines analytical chemistry through identification or composition analysis.
rubric.how: Define it as the branch that identifies substances and determines the composition or amount of their components.

rubric.why: Gives a practical use of analytical chemistry.
rubric.how: State that it is used to test purity, identify substances or measure their amounts in samples.

modelAnswer: Industrial chemistry is the branch of chemistry concerned with the manufacture of chemicals and useful products on a large scale.
It is used in the production of products such as fertilizers, medicines and cement.
Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry concerned with identifying substances and determining the composition or amount of their components.
It is used to test the purity and composition of materials, for example in quality control.

items.followUp: Write down five properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Awards a mark for the characteristic metallic lustre.
rubric.how: State that metals are generally lustrous or shiny.

rubric.why: Malleability is a characteristic physical property of metals.
rubric.how: State that metals can be hammered into thin sheets.

rubric.why: Ductility is another characteristic physical property.
rubric.how: State that metals can be drawn into wires.

rubric.why: Awards a mark for electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: State that metals generally conduct electricity.

rubric.why: Awards a mark for thermal conductivity.
rubric.how: State that metals generally conduct heat well.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
They are malleable and can be hammered into thin sheets.
They are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
They generally conduct electricity well.
They generally conduct heat well.

items.followUp: Discuss four factors that affect the rate of diffusion in gases.

rubric.why: Temperature affects the kinetic energy and speed of liquid particles.
rubric.how: Explain that increasing temperature makes particles move faster, increasing the rate of diffusion.

rubric.why: A greater difference in concentration drives faster net diffusion.
rubric.how: Explain that a greater concentration difference between regions increases the rate of diffusion.

rubric.why: Particle size influences how readily particles move through a liquid.
rubric.how: Explain that smaller particles generally diffuse faster than larger particles.

rubric.why: The liquid medium affects particle movement and therefore diffusion rate.
rubric.how: Explain that diffusion is faster through a less viscous liquid and slower through a more viscous liquid.

modelAnswer: Temperature: Raising the temperature increases the kinetic energy and speed of particles, so diffusion becomes faster.
Concentration difference: A greater concentration difference between two regions increases the rate of diffusion.
Particle size: Smaller particles generally diffuse faster than larger particles.
Nature of the liquid: Diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid and slower in a more viscous liquid.

rubric.why: Identifies inorganic chemistry as a branch of chemistry concerned with compounds.
rubric.how: State that inorganic chemistry is a branch of chemistry dealing with the study of inorganic compounds.

rubric.why: Distinguishes its subject matter from most carbon compounds studied in organic chemistry.
rubric.how: Explain that it mainly deals with elements and their compounds other than most carbon compounds.

modelAnswer: Inorganic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies elements and their compounds, other than most carbon compounds studied in organic chemistry.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: A compound consists of elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.how: State that a compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

rubric.why: Awards a mark for a valid example of a compound.
rubric.how: Give a valid example, such as water, sodium chloride or carbon dioxide.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Water (H₂O) is an example of a compound.
